title: The Reformed distinguish proximate and active power from remote and passive power (Pareus)
source_text: XXVI. Illud quoque hic observandum est Scholae Reformatae Doctores in hac quaestione distinguere inter potentiam proximam & activam, & inter potentiam remotam & passivam. Et concedunt hominem in statu peccati, & ante gratiam, habere quidem potentiam quandam remotam & passivam ad actus spirituales & supernaturales, sed negant hominem ita consideratum ad eosdem actus habere potentiam ullam proximam & activam. Qua distinctione utitur Paraeus in lib. 6. Bellar. de Lib. Arbitr. cap. 15.
pass_a_gloss: XXVI. This also is to be observed here, that the Doctors of the Reformed School in this question distinguish between proximate and active power, and between remote and passive power. And they grant that man in the state of sin, and before grace, has indeed a certain remote and passive power for spiritual and supernatural acts, but they deny that man so considered has any proximate and active power for the same acts. Which distinction Pareus uses on book 6 of Bellarmine on Free Choice chapter 15.
pass_b_english: A further point: on this question the Reformed doctors separate two kinds of capacity, the proximate and active kind and the remote and passive kind.

Man in the state of sin and before grace, they allow, keeps some remote, passive capacity for spiritual and supernatural acts; what they refuse him, so considered, is any proximate, active capacity for them. Pareus draws exactly this line when commenting on Bellarmine's sixth book on free choice, chapter 15.

lemmas.latin: habere quidem potentiam quandam remotam & passivam
lemmas.gloss: has indeed a certain remote and passive power

choices.why: The Schools' distinction between a remote (merely capable) and a proximate (ready to act) power; kept as technical terms.
